blocks.x: Do you want to ask me something?
Sure. I'd like to know your full name, please.
Well, you mean my married name or from childhood or what?
From childhood and married both.
Well, I was Mary Nadal, N-A, capital D-A-L. And I've never been married but once, and that was through Robert Hoffman and that's what I've been all these years since 1940.
That's capital N-A, small n.
No, capital N and then a capital D-A-L.
N-A-D-A-L with a capital N and a capital D. It's a name that I'd never heard before.
Well, I don't know what anybody else ever did. Not either. And I don't know why. My father was a Kentucky man. And I don't know about the name really.

Move these earphones out of the way. All right. Sometimes they get too close to the microphone and it gives you a little funny noise there. A little, yeah. Well, you've told me your age once when the machine is off. Do you mind my asking it again?
Oh, no. I'm 87. I was 87 on the fourth day of December.
And let's see, what year would that make you?
And where were you born? I was born in Frankfort, Kentucky.
Uh-huh. Did you grow up there?

No. 1888. So, when I was in the second grade at school, my mother moved to Louisville, Kentucky. And we lived there for about, oh, I don't know whether it was two years. Couldn't have been two or three years, something like that. And my father moved to Greenville, Mississippi. So, that's where I grew up. That's where I went to school and graduated from high school. And at that time, my mother died. And I really went back to Hopkinsville, Kentucky and went to a college up there where my father had sent my younger brother and sister. And I went, where do I go from there?
Oh, well, it was your family musical. Huh?

No. Nobody, I never heard of anybody in my family ever singing a note or playing a note or anything. But, when we moved to Greenville, Mississippi, we moved into a furnished house that had a piano in the living room. And sitting on that piano was a sheet, a book of like, Mama's Waltz, Papa's Waltz, Grandma's Waltz. I don't know who it belonged to at all. And I knew from going to school in Louisville, they taught little children to read the treble clef and to sing the parts. And so, we had already started the school. I took a piece of paper over, I didn't know the bass, you understand. I didn't know what the bass notes were at all. So, I took this piece of music over to the school and I asked the music teacher if she would show me on the piano. I mean, I should have said I made five lines on it and I made a note on the bottom line. And I asked if she'd show me where that note was on the piano. So, she did. And I took it back and I learned all those pieces in that book without, I have no ear actually. I shouldn't say I have no ear, but I don't have much of an ear for music. I can't play, remember pieces, I mean to hear pieces and then play. I can't do that. But I did learn to play all those pieces in that book. And at that time then, some of the people, the music teachers in town began to ask my mother if I couldn't take lessons. So, I took lessons from a lady there for a few months. And I don't remember what happened to her, but then a little time passed and then another lady I started taking music lessons from. I don't even remember the names. And I took lessons from her about five months. In the meantime, well, a little before that, my mother had bought a piano from a company in, I can't think of the name of that company in Memphis now. And as I was coming down the street, I saw a piano being moved into the house where my father had bought and we were living. And so, I went there, went in and there, my mother shook her finger in my face and she said, if anybody ever asks you to play and you say no, out goes the piano.
Oh, my.

So, you can imagine, well, that's the way it happened. And I didn't take any more lessons because of my mother's long illness and various, various things until I went away to college and I did study just one year there. So, that's all the training or the musical instructions I ever had. And the rest of it I just learned by doing, I guess. I don't know what else. I never, as I said, I never was a pianist to say that I was a skilled pianist. But I, I, um, when I started with the organ, that's another, that's where my husband came into the picture. Uh, let me see, how is this about there? Where was I working?
Where was I working?

Oh, I think it was when I was still playing at the Crest Doa. He had come back to New Orleans. He was a New Orleans man, alright, but he had been off somewhere else playing. And he came back into town and, um, uh, do you remember, do you know who Benny Mars was? A, a band leader that used to direct?
Yes, I know about him. Yeah, about him.

Well, he and my husband were friends. So, Benny Mars used to come into the store to get professional copies to the Crest store, yeah. And, uh, so one day he came in with this man and he introduced him to me. And, uh, so in talking, uh, Mr. Hoffman had started taking organ lessons from Bode Mala. Do you know who he was? He was, he was, uh, organist, uh, for the, uh, Jewish temple that's there on Carondelet Street where they, motion picture company.
I've seen his, I've seen his name. Uh-huh, Bode Mala.

Well, anyway, he was taking organ lessons from him. So, he said to me, if you will, he says, the coming thing in pictures is the organ. So, he says, if you'll get your organ to practice on, I'll teach you what Bode Mala teaches me. So, he got a book and gave it to me and I was, uh, going to the Christian church. That was my, really, home church, church I was, uh, raised in, up on St. Charles Avenue. And they said I could use the organ if they had a practice on. So, that's what I did. And pretty soon I got a job with, um, um, Fitchinburg, who was the first picture show people in town. I don't know that. Fitchinburg. And, um, when I look, I have a scrapbook. Oh. And I, I feel sure that I have, uh, in that scrapbook, I, I can show it to you. You can look at it as little or as much of it as you want to. Yeah. And it is, uh, a letterhead from Fitchinburg here. And, uh, they owned a place, uh, a picture show on the corner of Canal and Dortheen where Kassin Brestoff now sits. And Kassin Brestoff was next door. And this picture show was on the corner. And, um, so, uh, Mr. Hoffman, after I had, uh, of course, they, they didn't have an organ in that picture show. It was what was called an orgotron. It was a piano with two and a half octaves of organ that you played your right hand on. So, uh, he told me one day that, uh, the lady who played there had quit the night before. And why didn't I go down and ask for the job? So, I found out the man, that, in the meantime, I don't know whether Sanger had actually entered the field right at that moment or not. I don't remember that. But the manager had an office up over that picture show. And it's Mr. Geringer. Do you know that name?
I know the name again. Geringer, all right.

Well, so, I got up nerve enough, as inexperienced as I was and everything, to go there to ask him, uh, to tell him that I heard that the lady who played there had quit the night before and that, uh, I would like to get the job. And as I walked up, no, went up in a little elevator that ran up, you know who Carl Goldenberg is? Carl Goldenberg, he later was either the owner or the manager of one of the big bakeries here.
I don't know that name at all.

All right. All right. I frequented the store when I played the piano in the store. And, uh, when I walked in and, and he worked for, for Fichtenberg. Fichtenberg was his uncle. So, Carl worked for the, the uncle. So, he went up in this elevator at the same time I did. He says, what are you doing in here? I said, well, I've come here to ask Mr. Geringer for a job. And so, I went in to see Mr. Geringer and Mr. Geringer said, did you ever play in a picture show? And Carl Goldenberg walked in and told the biggest film anybody ever told. He said, oh, sure she did. She played in a picture show in Memphis. So, he gave me the job. It wasn't that awful.
Well, it worked out.

It worked. It worked. So, anyway, that's from that. I, I, uh, oh, the union was involved. And, and, uh, I did join the union. And then, Fichtenberg, I think, got angry with the union. And fired everybody that was union. And then across the street, on Canal, where, about where, um, where, uh, God Show is, was a picture show owned by Pierce Company. I don't know whether it was a company or not Pierce, anyway. And it was the Trianon. So, I, I got the job playing the organ, real sure enough, organ over there. And, uh, played there. Uh, actually, I don't remember until I went to work for Sanger then. And they had a show up on, uh, St. Charles, the Liberty, I believe was the name of it.
I've heard of it.
Where, um, Max Fink had an orchestra up there. Yes.
And they had a big organ.
Well, I played there, because I don't remember how long at all.
Was that where the orchestra, or a solo?

No, uh, organ, uh, played when the orchestra was not playing. I see. Uh, but sometimes, uh, once in a great while, a picture that came out would have a score with it. And there might, might be some time in that way you, you, you played as the orchestra did. I don't remember that that was done at, uh, at, um, the Liberty. But, uh, it did, uh, later, uh, uh, when the Strand opened up and got the main to direct the Greek orchestra that they had named Don Filippini, uh, we also would, well, occasionally would have a score, you know, so that, just once in a while, we played at the same time.
Yes.

Now, I have in here, uh, a few of the, um, uh, uh, I'll go easy. See this? Yeah. This is, uh, printed up there myself when I first got this scrapbook, of course, many years of the year. And, and this is my first, this is where, when I graduated from high school, I was a singer in those days. So, uh, I sang this, uh, if, if you, let's put up that shade a little bit. All right.
Let's see, that's, that's dated 1906.

Yes, that's the year I graduated. Oh, well, that won't, that won't hurt. That won't, that won't hurt. That's all right. It won't hurt her at all. Yeah. But, um, yes, this was the Granville High School. And, uh, if you see here, Mary Nadal. Mm-hmm. It's Josephine's daughter. Mm-hmm. Josephine, the captain's daughter of the...
That's kind of fun.
Uh-huh. So, uh, then these are just things that have nothing to do with, that's, this is, uh, these are, now there is a, um, I think that's a two cent stamp on that car, maybe even a one cent stamp.
A two cent, isn't it?
Uh-huh. That's, I can, that, that date must be something around, uh, 1909 or eight or something like that.
It was copyrighted in 1907, but I can't, well, I can't read the postmark.
Well, anyway, it's long about that time. These are just other...
I think it's 1907, it looks like.

These are just other things that, that I, this was my father's, uh, picture. He was a, a, a towboat captain and pilot. Mm-hmm. And, uh, that was a, right, or something. Mm-hmm. These are different towns I've lived in, and I sang, I had a job singing in this church. Uh, after I got out of college, I stayed in Hopkinsville and worked for a while.
What was the name of the college, by the way? I'm sorry.
It, it's, oh, it burned down years and years ago, and it's not known since. It was the, McLean, McLean College. I'm just, uh, uh, now here's just...
Oh, that's wonderful.
The time I attended the, uh, French opera was to see this, uh, Cavalier Rusticana and Pagliacci. And, uh, let's see...
That must have been right before it burned. It was.

It was almost immediately before. Now this is, this is a little interesting thing. There was a, um, a lawyer in this town named Mr. W. O. Hart. I think his name is on this. And they had a Constitutional Convention dinner. See, reunion and banquet of members of the Constitutional Convention in the years. And it was in the gold room of the Grunewald Hotel, May the 22nd, 1915. And Mr. Hart knew, I don't, I don't even know how he knew or thought I could sing or what. But anyway, he engaged me to sing at this dinner. And, uh, all of this is, the music is scheduled according to what was being said and what they were talking about and everything. And what I sang was listen to the Mockingbird.
I see it in the city of New Orleans.

Uh-huh. And, uh, so, uh, we were, the musicians, there were other musicians besides me. Yeah. And we were behind curtains. And, uh, I like to tell that I got so much applause that I went back out and I sang, they told me to. I went back out in front and I sang Just a Little Love, A Little Kiss. You remember that song? I do not.
Beautiful French.

Uh, not, I don't mean, uh, written in French or anything, just a French song. And these are just about all the different places. Uh-huh. When I worked for Sangha, they sent me all, wherever they put in a new, opened up a new show and put in, uh, uh, a new organ, put in an organ. Why then, I would go and play for a couple of years or so until they get somebody to, um, fill the place. Uh, I have all kinds of things in here.
Yeah.
I want you to look at this. This is a mighty mushroom bursting through a concrete pavement.
Yeah. You just saved everything. Well, I, I. Anything of interest to you.
I've gotten to where I, uh, throw some things away now. But, uh, in different towns, I used to, uh, we used to put on amateur shows.
Oh, that's your name.

Yeah. See, uh, this other young lady and I put these, they would be benefits. Uh-huh. You know, in a small town, you could, uh, have it for some church or get something. And the picture show, that would go on as usual, and you sold the tickets and so forth and so on. So I did that in various, uh, towns where I was. This is some more of that same kind of thing. See, here's the, this one we put on the spring soiree. And, uh, these are just friends and different, different things. Oh, there was something, let's see, several injured. Oh, yes. I was moving from Yazoo City to Columbus, Mississippi, and some people ran into me and turned me over. So, that was what that was. And, uh, these are just all things like that. Everything, this is something that was in the paper one time. See, when I went, I think that was Columbus, Mississippi. I'm not quite sure.
There's a space between the A and the D in your name. The first A.
Well, that's not supposed to be.
Not supposed to be, they just did that.
No, no, no, they just, uh, different places, they wouldn't get it just right.
Yes. Now, wait a minute. Now, this is the prelude.
Prelude, so this, this is from Sanger. And, um...

We have that up at Tulane, that same magazine. Oh, do you? And we have it all indexed, where it tells about your husband. Oh. When he would serve, uh, as an official in the union, they would be putting on a ball or something.
Uh-huh, uh-huh.
I forget all the different things he did.

I don't even, let's see if there's anything in this one about... No, this is an article I wrote for it. Oh. Why noise and noise and organist. That was one of the greatest, uh, uh, troubles that we ever had, people who played the organ. Uh, young people would come in and, you know, and they'd all get cutting up and making noise and everything. Yeah. Maybe you'd be playing some beautiful, sad something and there would noise. So I wrote that. I don't even remember what it said. I haven't looked at it for a long time. These are... Oh, these are things. There's, uh... Don Philippine? Don Philippine.
Yeah.
Don Philippine. Yeah.
And he left town.
Yes, he, uh, he went to California and believe it or not, I lived in California for five years. I went into a store in Palm Springs and ran into him in that store. Hmm.
But you don't know the date here, do you? It doesn't have the date on it, does it?
Well, I don't know whether it's...
Well, I'm sure that the union has it written up. Uh... We could check the union records if we're after.
You mean for his tenure, uh...
Yeah, when he left, but if anybody's interested, they can look that up at the union.
Well, let's see. All right, um... This is just... Some man wanted me to come to work for him. He just wrote such a nice letter. Here's the, um, the program from the singer.
Mrs. Marguerite Clark lived here, didn't she?
Yes, yes, she lived.
She moved here.
But not during these years. Mm-hmm. See, see here, uh, I played there at the same time. Lorman was one of the organists that played there. I think that's his name there.
Ed Lorman. He was, he wrote a lot of stuff for Prelude too, and...
Oh, did he? Mm-hmm. Uh, this is, uh... You know, you know about this one too, huh?
No, the Sanger Humdinger. I've never seen that.

Uh-huh. Well, that's that, and... Oh. This is just a nice letter of math. This is from the State Tax Commission office in Mississippi, and I was playing in the picture show, and I met this man once later. He says, I am, uh, availing myself of my last opportunity to hear your beautiful music. I will appreciate, uh, your, any classic you will play, or, and then I'll, or something there. Uh, play for me, or some waltz you wanna play. Yeah. And I will also enjoy a little number, Wyoming... What is it? What is it?
I'm gonna unfold it, so it doesn't get... It'll break if you leave it. It will. It will. Wyoming waltz.

If you, I don't know whether I even knew it, and I don't remember whether I even knew it or not. Now, this was October, this is Greenville, Mississippi. Oh, that man first was in the picture show and went in Vicksburg one time. I didn't even remember it was in 23.
10th of October, and his name looks like Robert Feiffer.

Robert Feiffer was the, he was, uh, I don't remember his name's up here or not, but anyway, he was from this office. Yeah. That's what he happened to write on, or I wouldn't have... And more sang. Or Sanger. Here's another Sanger one. Mm-hmm. The C. L. Lorman.
And Elmore Russ, they have that. I don't, I'm not familiar with him. Who? Elmore Russ, I'm not familiar with him.
I'm not either. Elmore Russ. Oh! I don't remember him exactly. Now, when I lived in Natchez, this company came there and made a picture. Colleen Moore was a star of it. Do you remember her?
Yes.
Now, here's, uh, one of the Sanger. Is this, yes, this is a program, too.
Volume 3, number 43, it says, but it doesn't give the date, does it?
I think I was looking to see if I could find the date on any of these, but, uh, this was back in the teens. I know that. Mm-hmm.
Let's see.
It's a guarantee.
I hardly ever get this out anymore.
Yeah.
Here's Kitsch and Burr. Let's see what it says here. This one.

My first movie job in New Orleans. In Louisiana, I guess. In Louisiana, I guess. In Louisiana, 1914, with this firm. Mm-hmm. And, uh, I think it was a great thing. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Mm-hmm. That's my, my first movie job in New Orleans. In Louisiana, I guess. In Louisiana, in Louisiana, 1914, with this firm. Mm-hmm. Now, the other one where, um, where, um, Carl Goldenberg was the manager was this Alamo, which was on the street down, uh, out from there. And this Pico was a piano player that he and Bob had grown up together here in New Orleans. I didn't even know of him at this time, though.
He was in Vicksburg Pico, I see.
Pico.
Mm-hmm.
And, uh, he, um, ended up, for years and years and years living in San Antonio, Texas. Mm-hmm. And, uh, he ran a fix-it shop.
Oh, yeah.
And, uh, at the time my husband died, he was 86, Pico was long about that age, and that was a number of years ago, and I haven't, you know, I haven't heard anything of him.
That's the, uh, since then. See, they had a chain here. It looks like they've got the, uh.
Well, they had, see, the Alamo and the Plaza and the Dream World. Now, I never heard of this one. Pictou. I never heard of that one. I never heard of that one.
Must have been a tiny one.
See, uh, see, in the 19th. Oh, and then they had one in, um, Houston.
That's the Isis.
Alamo. And Pensacola.
And the Isis in Pensacola, too.

I didn't really realize that. Yeah. And, uh, this is just other friends and, and, uh, let's see what I have written there. It talks a world. Oh, this is about light being frozen and carried from one city to another. Uh-huh. So I, I've saved all kinds of things. Uh, all of this is getting dilapidated. Uh-huh.
Well, it's a...
It just does. It does.
Uh, there are ways of treating things like that and straightening them out, and I really should, uh...

Uh, oh, this is the kind of thing I like to drag out once in a while, because everybody thinks, not everybody, but most people think that, um, um, uh, what's the, what was the pilot, you know, the spirit of saying? Lindbergh. Lindbergh was the first person to fly there.
Yes.

Atlantic, and he wasn't. See, these two men were the first ones. Yeah. But he was the first to fly there alone. Yeah. And, uh, people forget that part of it. Uh-huh. And, uh, I was an admirer of O. O. McIntyre that wrote for the New York Times, and I used to, uh, save things. This was just something else from Tulsa. I guess I've gotten past anything about New Orleans here, because these were, were, uh, from later years.
You've really traveled.

Oh, well, yes, I've lived around a lot of places, and I've traveled. Just in the United States. I never have been out. Oh. This was a delightful thing that I attended one time in New York. A friend, uh, um, was the, um, Boy Scout director in a small town where I lived, and his little son went on this trip as, to, uh, one of the Scandinavian countries, you know, and they all met in New York, and I happened to, another girl and I happened to be up there in the summer, and, uh, we, um, I was invited. She wasn't because of other reasons, but I was invited to a banquet at the Commodore Hotel the night before they sailed on this, the ship, and it, there were, I think, 600 people there, and, honey, when they played Dixie and everybody stood up, I never died. That's 1928, I see.
Yeah. Down at the bottom. So that's, this is. Saturday, July the 28th, 1928. Mm-hmm.
But, uh, this is the, the trip and the names, I know that name is on there, but I, I think it's there.
There was something right underneath it I noticed about music. It says. Oh, you mean, oh.
From the Commercial Appeal.
Tommy Wright, Bunk and Junk.
Why are you looking right? Right underneath.
Blues is edited. Tommy, Tommy Wright.
Bunk and Junk.
Blues is a magazine of new rhythms. This is from the Memphis, no, no, it says the Commercial. Commercial Appeal.
That would be it.
Looks like a D. It does look like a D, but. It must be, maybe it says D. Wait a minute, wait a minute. Maybe we've got it right underneath here. Some more. But it talks about a magazine.
Oh, I, I really forgot that was in here. Uh-huh.
That's a, this is really fascinating stuff, isn't it?
Mm-hmm.
It's a shame there's no date on this. But it's too late now.
I bet you it would show on the other side of that. Yeah. Well, now, there may be something in the written part that would indicate or something. Yeah, well, I'll, I'll.
Well, we can.
Yeah. Uh, but I really don't know. Wait, go, see, if there is, I can't see that well enough. Well. I need to see something about rhythm and. Yes.
Well, we'll, we might be able to find that. That's falling to pieces, too. Oh, right. Oh, right. As a letter from, uh, O. Macintyre.
Here, here, here, let's see. Mm-hmm. I wrote, I, shame on you, Mr. Macintyre.
Oh, oh.

And he, uh, yeah, he said, Dear Mr. Dale, most grammatical, oh, Lord, um, something, but the original copy showed this. It, it, it, it was some error that was in the printed word. Yes. And he says the original shows it was correct. Uh-huh. I forgot what it was, even. Well. That was. We got a plague off. This is after I went to California, and I, these are just some things I saw out there. 1934, it says. December 23rd.
I went in, um, 34. Uh-huh.

This is during the Depression. Uh-huh. Of course, there was no more. Of course, uh, at the time I was in Columbus, Mississippi, is when I was in the place, when the talkies came in, and I just naturally lost my job, and there were no others. Yeah. You couldn't go somewhere else and work, you know. Yeah. Because everybody else was in the same fix. But, um, the rest of this is, um, um, different churches where I played, and, and this, this is a darling church I played in, and, uh, along, um, Lakewood Village, it was known as in those days, but it's a big city now. The, uh, town has grown to be a big, big place, right out of, uh, Long Beach. It says Lakewood Church.
Yes. That's in Mississippi.
There's, California.
Oh, California. California.
Oh, this was just something pertaining to a womanless wedding we put on one night. Oh, those used to be very funny.
Yes, they were.
They were. These are just different places I went out there. And, uh, they're up to Mount Wilson and Catalina, and, oh, I went, this is the picture of the, The mock wedding.
The mock, the, uh, yeah.

Womanless wedding. Mm-hmm. I have the, the original, the big, big sheet in there. But, um, see, I, I, I don't know, I still had some things, I guess, to put in, but I, you kind of lose interest, you know, after. Uh-huh. These are just, just things that I wrote myself that. Stories. Oh, I never did, oh, I never did do anything with them, but I, I used to fiddle around writing. I've written, um, since I've been at the church over here, I went to work there as a secretary, and, um, uh, two of the ladies in the church were getting out a church paper, and they asked me if I'd write something for it, and I said, I don't know anything to write. I never wrote anything for a paper in my life. So they said, well, write something out of your past. So I started writing, uh, a column, wrote it for years, called, Madam Secretary Speaks. And it was, um, sometimes it would be humorous, sometimes it would be funny things that happened to me, sometimes beautiful things, sometimes, uh, other more serious subjects. But I wrote it for years, and, uh, I always, I always liked to write. I think if I had had the proper training in the beginning, you know, as a young, young person, and known it, known it, I didn't even know that I liked to write when I was, really, say, in my teens or anything like that, I never thought of it. But afterward, I, I like to put things down on paper. So, that's that.

It's about to, the tape's about to run off now. And, and, it always, just when I want to ask you a question about something, that's when the tape runs off. Oh, it is to the end. Yeah, it's just about to the end now.
I know you and boy interested in the things about .
Yes, I have the second reel on there, Ms. Hoffman, and it's going. So, let's see how it sounds. I was going to ask you about going to Memphis. Going to Memphis? You mean my original...

Tulane. Yes, I work up there at Tulane and we'll keep these up there for anybody who wants to hear them. Oh. So we've got the fourth reel on in which you give me your history and your husband's history. It's a way of... Oh boy, it's really mixed up, isn't it? Well, we have to do our best on it. We were talking about rags and you were talking about some... Can you play any of his rags like Pussyfoot rag or Black Hand? You never played those, huh? Did he play them later? No, but honey, you can

understand that playing in a picture show, you're not playing that type of things in the first place. No. You're not playing Maple Leaf and Cannonball and those things. Those are things that I've more or less just since in the last few years have put up there on the piano and started playing. I've had such a mixed up career and then you get to playing in church. See, I played over here in this church before I went to work there in the office and well, I played for years in the church. I don't even know. Well, the honey up there on that wall, there's our two plaques that were given to me. I saw them. I was going to mention that. As a matter of fact, no, I put both from the Gentile Presbyterian Church. Yeah, one was for the organ and the other the office.

Mm-hmm. I see. Well, that's a lot of fun. Well, anyway, when he quit playing in theaters and things, did he play his own pieces at home? When he'd entertain people at the church, would he play his own pieces? No. That's funny. He was timid, you say.

Well, I think my husband, he was a soft-voiced kind of man and he was timid. I can't think of any better word to describe. And how you know some people are the salesman type. Yeah.
